title: The simile of the saw
hookLine: even if bandits sawed you limb from limb, keep a mind of goodwill (MN 21)
last: CROWBAR — A TOOL KEPT FOR LAST.

cards: A monk named Moliya Phagguna spent a great deal of time with the nuns. When anyone criticized the nuns in front of him, he got angry and argued. When anyone criticized him in front of them, they got angry and argued.
Word of it reached the Buddha. And what he said, first to Phagguna and then to all the monks, builds to a sentence that is hard to hear.

teach.b: MN 21, the Kakacupama. The Buddha tells Phagguna: whatever anyone says, about the nuns or about you, train like this. My mind will not be changed.
I won't utter harsh words. I'll stay compassionate, with a mind of goodwill, without inner hate.
Then he lays out five ways people may speak to you: at the right time or the wrong time, truly or falsely, gently or harshly, helpfully or not, with goodwill or with hate.
Any of the five may come; the training stays the same. Then pictures, one after another. A man comes with a hoe and a basket to make the great earth not-earth.
He digs, he scatters, he spits. He can't do it; the earth is too vast.
So abide with a mind like the earth: vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility.

teach.h: PAINT ON SPACE, BURN THE GANGES.
teach.b: Someone tries to paint pictures on empty space; there's nothing for the paint to cling to. Someone tries to boil the river Ganges with a blazing grass torch.
Someone rubs a soft, well-cured catskin bag and tries to make it crackle. None of it works. And last, the hard sentence.

teach.h: EVEN WITH A SAW: NO HATE.
teach.b: Even if bandits were to cut you apart, limb by limb, with a two-handled saw, whoever let their mind turn to hate because of it would not be carrying out the teaching.
It's the extreme case, set at the end as the floor. The Dhammapada says it in an old line, in Max Müller's translation: “hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love.”

how: Teachers cite the simile of the saw when they teach patience, and some pair it with loving-kindness meditation directed toward difficult people.

o: a carpenter's guide to cutting timber
a tale of a saw that cuts by itself
the simile of the saw: no hate, even then

p: angry when the nuns were criticized

s: the five ways of speech include speech with hate behind it
timely or untimely, true or false, gentle or harsh, helpful or not, kind or hateful.
MN 21 says hate is justified if the attack is cruel enough
even under the saw, hate isn't carrying out the teaching.
the Dhammapada says hatred ceases by love
the verse itself calls it an old rule.

games.q: someone tries to boil the river Ganges with a blazing grass torch. what happens, in MN 21?
o: nothing: the river is far too vast
games.why: the torch can't touch it. a mind made vast with goodwill is like that: the harsh word has nothing to burn.

practice: Bring to mind one person who criticizes you, not the worst one, someone manageable, and notice what the body does.

Then picture the earth under you, wide and unbothered, taking footsteps and rain alike, and see if you can wish that critic one ordinary good thing, like a good night's sleep. If you can't today, that's honest; the earth can wait.

wordCard.voice: Kakacupama, the simile of the saw. Even under the cruelest treatment, keep a mind of goodwill, vast and steady as the earth.

orig.note: Pali kakacūpama: the simile of the saw; kakaca is a saw.

carryVoice: Your line: a mind like the earth. Wide enough that a sharp word has room to land. That's day four hundred seventeen.

sources.q: hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love
